title: Math Professor and NFL Player, He Says He Was Just Lucky
dek: John Urschel played in the NFL while finishing an MIT math PhD, yet says talent is only a small part — his success came from ‘an enormous amount of hard work’ and luck. He even hopes his football fame didn't get him his MIT job.
why: This is the audio version of a video interview, so the information density isn't high, but Urschel talking about how he crammed two full-time jobs into the same week, and why he ultimately quit football, is worth listening to.
who: Suitable for founders and engineers interested in ‘doing two hard things at once’, especially those who want to know how to fit two full-time jobs into the same week, and when to give one up.
skip: The first two minutes on childhood and family background can be skipped; start listening from the 08:16 coach conversation.

points.h: A coach's joke made him realize he could make the NFL
points.body: After Urschel's junior season, his position coach called him in, meaning ‘don't think about anything crazy, stay another year’ — crazy meaning declaring early for the draft. He wasn't thinking about the NFL at all at the time, but that sentence made him realize for the first time: this thing would happen if he wanted it. Later the coach would say in practice ‘they (the league) will like this move’. He didn't rely on confidence; he relied on others assuming he belonged at that level.

points.h: He first asked his coach about a PhD; the coach thought he already had a degree
points.body: Urschel did an MIT math PhD while playing in the NFL. He says he ‘didn't cheat’ because he asked coach John Harbaugh beforehand whether he could go back to school for a degree. The coach replied ‘absolutely support, we support players finishing their education’, then a minute later added a text: ‘I thought you already had a degree and a master's.’ Urschel replied: ‘But I don't have a PhD.’ The coach replied ‘oh, okay’, and that was approval. He picked courses with no exams that he could pass by reading the textbook, three PhD courses a semester.

points.h: On planes he pretended his math book was a chess book
points.body: During the NFL season almost all his time each day went to football, and at night he watched film to prepare. Math could only be done when others relaxed — like on team flights, when everyone was watching movies. He says if he were reading a chess book it would be totally fine, but reading a math book was ‘a bit suspicious’, and teammates might think he was too distracted, so he would say ‘it's not a math book, it's a chess book’, flip it open for them, and they'd say ‘okay’. The real solution was: he finished the textbooks before the semester started, otherwise it would have been impossible.

points.h: The CTE controversy conveniently gave him cover to retire
points.body: The host asked whether the years when CTE (brain damage from repeated head hits) became an NFL headline happened to coincide with when he was considering retirement. Urschel said ‘it gave me very good cover’. But he also said he was worried before that. He was weighing whether to play another season, the last year of his rookie contract, with the next contract at least in the million-dollar-a-year range, while his first-year base salary was 420,000. He once convinced himself to stay with ‘the contract has one year left, I'll fulfill it’ — the same mindset as when he honored his commitment to Penn State.

points.h: Looking back, he doesn't know what he was agonizing over
points.body: Urschel says looking back now, agonizing over retirement made little sense: the team could cut him at any time, the contract wasn't guaranteed, and injury would end it. What he really cared about then was math and his newborn child, both rising in importance, while football ranked third yet was a real burden on the first two — not just the head, but the whole body, whether he could still walk at 50, whether he could pick up grandchildren and his daughter. He said ‘I needed to retire, focus on math, and go be with my child’.

points.h: He estimates only 4% of Americans like math
points.body: The host asked him to guess how many out of 100 Americans like math. Urschel said if you define ‘math’ as the general public understands it, 4% might even be high. The host said that number is a bit sad. Urschel's own definition is broad: math is the quantitative language we all share for reasoning about problems; engineering, theoretical physics, statistics, theoretical computer science all count as math, not far from doing puzzles, not far from the goal of ‘understanding something’.

points.h: His daughter can't play football; his son must show he truly needs it
points.body: Asked whether his two children should play football, Urschel said his daughter shouldn't — he won't accept that level of risk. For his son, if it looks like something he ‘really needs to do’, he would allow it. He explained what need means: football suits young people who crave and benefit from ‘consensual violence, controlled, mutually agreed aggression’ — with rules, not trying to hurt people, essentially a proxy for war. He says it was very good for the combative high schooler he was. If it's just ‘because dad played’ or ‘because all my friends play’, he'd have the kid try wrestling or judo first.

points.h: He says he actually had no talent as an NFL player
points.body: The host praised him for being good at several hard things at once. Urschel said talent does play a role, but compared to NFL players he ‘had no talent’ — he admits he has some athletic gifts, like broad shoulders, but in the league that doesn't count. So how did he succeed? ‘Hard work, an enormous amount of hard work.’ The source is ‘wanting to be better’. Asked whether his MIT job came from football fame, he said ‘I don't know, I hope not’.
